Introduction to Singly LinkedList.theory: A node stores a value and a next reference; a doubly node also stores prev. Head is a reference to the first node, null for empty. These linked-list lessons use a shared teaching Node with optional random/bottom fields; only the links needed by the operation are meaningful. Arrays give O(1) indexed access, lists require O(n) traversal. Inserting/deleting at a known predecessor is O(1), but locating position k is O(n). Always save the suffix before overwriting next and assign the returned head. Doubly splices update both directions. The concrete head, tail, kth, given-value and given-node lessons in this subsection contain executable implementations and worked examples. For DLL verification, additionally traverse backward from tail and check every reciprocal link.

Traversal in Linked List.problem: Read values by following next until null.
Traversal in Linked List.approach: Each iteration visits exactly the next node; no array index is involved.
Traversal in Linked List.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state (head insertion/deletion are O(1)); returned view string/list allocates O(n).
Traversal in Linked List.trace: Run the demo and draw one box per value; trace predecessor, current and next before each link update. The expected output below shows the resulting chain.
Traversal in Linked List.pitfalls: Methods assume finite acyclic input. Return values must be assigned to retain changed heads. Singly operations maintain next links only; prev is irrelevant here. Odd/even grouping means index parity, not value parity.

Convert Array to Doubly Linked List.problem: Perform the named operation on a doubly linked list; kth positions are ONE-based. Given-node parameters must actually belong to the list. Return and retain the new head.
Convert Array to Doubly Linked List.approach: Maintain the invariant p.next.prev==p wherever p.next exists, and p.prev.next==p wherever p.prev exists. Head.prev is null and tail.next is null. Inserting links both neighbors to the new node; deleting reconnects both neighbors and detaches the removed node. Reversal swaps both links at every node.
Convert Array to Doubly Linked List.complexity: O(n) when traversal/conversion/deduplication is needed; O(1) for a known-node splice or head operation. Conversion allocates O(n) output nodes; other operations use O(1) auxiliary state.
Convert Array to Doubly Linked List.trace: Draw the demo chain with arrows in both directions. Apply the splice or swap shown in solve; confirm both forward and backward adjacency after each operation.
Convert Array to Doubly Linked List.pitfalls: Updating only next produces a broken doubly list. Null, singleton and head/tail cases need explicit handling. Duplicate removal requires sorted input.

Add two numbers in Linked List.problem: Each list represents a nonnegative integer with LEAST-significant digit first. Return a new list for their sum; inputs are not modified.
Add two numbers in Linked List.approach: Add corresponding digits plus carry; output sum%10 and propagate sum/10. Missing digits act as zero; a final carry needs one more node.

Add two numbers in Linked List.pitfalls: This digit order differs from Add One. Empty plus empty returns an empty representation of zero.

Check if LL is palindrome or not.approach: Find first-half tail, reverse the second half, compare corresponding values, then reverse that half back. Compare only while the second half has nodes to ignore an odd center.

Find the intersection point of Y LL.problem: Return the shared NODE of two acyclic chains, or null. Equal values alone do not count as intersection.
Find the intersection point of Y LL.approach: Switch each pointer to the other head after its first null. Both traverse the same total distance a+b, aligning their shared suffix; they meet at the entry or both null.
Find the intersection point of Y LL.trace: Prefixes of length 1 and 2 join the same 8->9 objects; switching heads aligns the pointers at 8.
Find the intersection point of Y LL.pitfalls: No mutation is needed. Cyclic lists require a different intersection analysis.

Detect a loop in LL.problem: Detect a cycle, return its entry VALUE (-1 absent), or count its length as indicated by the title. The reusable entry method returns the node identity.
Detect a loop in LL.approach: Floyd slow/fast pointers meet if a cycle exists. After meeting, resetting one pointer to head and moving both one step locates the entry. Walking one lap from entry gives cycle length.
Detect a loop in LL.trace: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 2... has entry node 2 and cycle length 2.
Detect a loop in LL.pitfalls: Compare node identity, not equal values. Do not call view on a cyclic list. The -1 VALUE adapter is ambiguous for negative node values; use entry directly.
Detect a loop in LL.alternatives: A HashSet of visited node identities uses O(n) storage.

Reverse LL in group of given size K.problem: Reverse each FULL block of k nodes; leave a final short block unchanged.
Reverse LL in group of given size K.approach: First verify k nodes exist, remember the following suffix, then reverse exactly up to that suffix. Reconnect the block and advance its predecessor to the former first node.
Reverse LL in group of given size K.trace: Blocks [1,2] and [3,4] reverse; trailing [5] stays unchanged.
Reverse LL in group of given size K.pitfalls: Some platforms reverse the short final group too; this implementation explicitly preserves it.

Rotate a LL.approach: Create a ring, locate the node before the new head at position n-k, then break the ring.
Rotate a LL.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state (head insertion/deletion are O(1)); returned view string/list allocates O(n).
Rotate a LL.trace: Run the demo and draw one box per value; trace predecessor, current and next before each link update. The expected output below shows the resulting chain.
Rotate a LL.pitfalls: Methods assume finite acyclic input. Return values must be assigned to retain changed heads. Singly operations maintain next links only; prev is irrelevant here. Odd/even grouping means index parity, not value parity.

Merge two Sorted Lists.problem: Merge two disjoint sorted acyclic chains by relinking their nodes.
Merge two Sorted Lists.approach: Repeatedly take the smaller head. It is the smallest remaining value globally; append the surviving suffix when one chain ends.
Merge two Sorted Lists.pitfalls: Inputs must not share nodes, or relinking can create cycles. Equality takes from the first list, preserving stable order.

Flattening of LL.problem: Heads linked by next each own a sorted bottom chain. Merge into one sorted bottom chain, clearing next links.
Flattening of LL.approach: Recursively flatten the head suffix, then merge its bottom chain with the current one. The sorted-chain merge invariant preserves global order.
Flattening of LL.complexity: O(N*k) worst time for N total nodes in k columns; O(k) recursion stack.
Flattening of LL.pitfalls: This multi-level sorted bottom representation differs from depth-first flattening of a doubly list. Node identities are reused.
Flattening of LL.alternatives: A min-heap over k chain fronts gives O(N log k) time/O(k) auxiliary space.

Sort LL.problem: Stable nondecreasing linked-list sort by relinking nodes.
Sort LL.approach: Split the chain at its midpoint, disconnect halves, recursively sort, then merge. Split makes progress even for two nodes because fast starts at h.next.
Sort LL.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(log n) recursion stack.
Sort LL.pitfalls: Forgetting to disconnect slow.next prevents the subproblem from shrinking. Singly next links are maintained.

Clone a LL with random and next pointer.problem: Deep-copy an acyclic next chain whose random pointers are null or point within that chain. Restore original next links.
Clone a LL with random and next pointer.approach: Interleave each copy after its original. Then original.random.next is the corresponding copied random target. Finally separate original and copied chains.
Clone a LL with random and next pointer.complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space excluding O(n) new output nodes.
Clone a LL with random and next pointer.trace: A->A'->B->B'; A'.random is B', B'.random is A'; split back into two chains.
Clone a LL with random and next pointer.pitfalls: Random references must lie inside the chain. The method temporarily mutates original next links, so concurrent traversal is unsafe.
Clone a LL with random and next pointer.alternatives: A map original->copy supports a simpler O(n)-space two-pass implementation.

Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL.problem: Perform the named operation on a doubly linked list; kth positions are ONE-based. Given-node parameters must actually belong to the list. Return and retain the new head.
Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL.approach: Maintain the invariant p.next.prev==p wherever p.next exists, and p.prev.next==p wherever p.prev exists. Head.prev is null and tail.next is null. Inserting links both neighbors to the new node; deleting reconnects both neighbors and detaches the removed node. Reversal swaps both links at every node.
Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL.complexity: O(n) when traversal/conversion/deduplication is needed; O(1) for a known-node splice or head operation. Conversion allocates O(n) output nodes; other operations use O(1) auxiliary state.
Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL.trace: Draw the demo chain with arrows in both directions. Apply the splice or swap shown in solve; confirm both forward and backward adjacency after each operation.
Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL.pitfalls: Updating only next produces a broken doubly list. Null, singleton and head/tail cases need explicit handling. Duplicate removal requires sorted input.

Find Pairs with Given Sum in Doubly Link.problem: A nondecreasing DLL; return unique VALUE pairs from two distinct nodes that sum to target.
Find Pairs with Given Sum in Doubly Link.approach: Move the lower pointer forward if sum is low, upper backward if high. On equality emit and skip equal endpoint values. Stop when pointers meet or cross.
Find Pairs with Given Sum in Doubly Link.complexity: O(n) time; O(number of pairs) output space.
Find Pairs with Given Sum in Doubly Link.trace: 1+5=6, then 2+4=6; pointers meet at 3, which cannot pair with itself.
Find Pairs with Given Sum in Doubly Link.pitfalls: Track pointer positions as well as references so skipping duplicate runs stops safely when positions cross. Two separate equal-valued nodes can form a pair; one node cannot pair with itself.

Append to Doubly Linked List.problem: Append one new value, preserving both next and prev links.
Append to Doubly Linked List.approach: Locate tail, connect tail.next to new node and new.prev to tail; empty input becomes the new node.
Append to Doubly Linked List.complexity: O(n) traversal time, O(1) auxiliary space plus one new node.
Append to Doubly Linked List.pitfalls: Maintaining a separate tail field would make repeated append O(1). Head-only API scans each time.
